utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as you have given me a very short period of time to ask my questions, I can only ask a few. But I should like to draw your attention and have you understand with respect to the events that the witness is testifying about that from the document on the Muslim side, which I received from the opposing party there pursuant to Rule 68, and it is page 01025180, on that page it talks about the events in Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992. And from that document, one can see that they were in fact local paramilitary forces. That is evident from that document. I just wish to give you this as reference - I quoted the page number - for it to be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask the witness about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I referred to their own document to make this clear to you and to throw light upon the answers given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B-1701, in your previous statement you said that these people were killed by a woman from Kravica. Why did you change that assertion of yours and why do you then go on to speak of the fact that it was the army that did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have maintained, I said when it began on the 9th of May, that genocide, it was the women. They worked together. And I stand by it. She was a soldier. She was wearing a Yugoslav People's Army uniform, and I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. In paragraph 13 of your statement, you say: "In my previous statement it says that a woman killed them from Kravica. But I should like to explain here that I didn't see her actually firing."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see her personally fire when she fired at that young person Mensur, but I saw personally her fire at Camil, and then she turned from Camil towards Mensur and I think she shot him. Nobody else did. Because as soon as she turned towards me, her pistol was raised up in the air like that and I saw the smoke or whatever coming out of the barrel, so I was able to conclude that nobody else had fired except her. And she was a soldier of the Yugoslav People's Army and was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And a moment ago, I asked you whether you knew that it was the local paramilitary unit. And in the document itself which has come in to us from the Muslim side, it names names and identifies the people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any of these paramilitary units. All I can do is recognise the Yugoslav People's Army unit, and that is the army, as far as I'm concerned, and I recognise nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say you know -- knew the woman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the woman. She was a cleaning lady at Potocari in a company there, in a transport company. And I knew her by sight. I didn't socialise with her, but I knew her by sight. I knew her like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the woman's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't know the name. I can't tell you the name. I'd be lying if I said I could, and I don't wish to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I quite respect that, but you're talking about a woman, and then you say -- and you say you didn't mention the army, and then suddenly afterwards you mention the army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very first moment she was with the army and she was wearing a uniform, from the first, and that's what she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say the army, do you mean that woman too? Do you include that woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. She was a soldier too, and it was all the army, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to enumerate other people, somebody nicknamed Riba Milo, Zaric, Radic, Pera, and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people I saw around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you name several people there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are they all people from your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all in the municipality. They were all my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I wanted to hear. They were all your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Bratunac municipality. I recognise the people. I didn't see them do anything; I didn't see them beat anyone or provoke anyone or things like that, I don't want to say that. No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this happened on the 9th of May; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were conflicts -- I mentioned Bijecevo, that is a neighbouring village, where various Serbs were killed on the 6th of May, for example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then again on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, how could I know that? I said yesterday that I was in such a bad state that I was urinating blood and I had to hide in a bunker. That is to say I hid in the ground. I dug out a hole and it was like a bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you, are you aware of the fact that the conflict was two-sided, and quite obviously -- and I have a piece of information here which I received from the opposite side over there, Mr. May. And it is page 017975, where we can see the 6th of May, the 7th of May, the 8th of May, the 9th of May, and that includes the day when this particular event took place, the one that the witness is testifying about. So I'm asking you whether you know that there were conflicts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you alleging? You say you have this piece of paper. We don't know what it is. And then you say we can see the 6th, the 7th, and the 8th of May. Now, what are you alleging occurred on those days? So clarify that so the witness can understand what you're putting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on those days that there were clashes, that clashes took place, and I have a list of the casualties, the victims. And it says, "Provisional List of Victims of Muslim Terror Over the Serbian People." That's the title of the document. And then it says April 1992, in May, the 6th of May, the 7th of May, 8th of May, 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who put this forward? What is this document that you're referring to? Can you help us, Mr. Groome? It's apparently one of your documents that you disclosed to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their numbering is 01 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to try to pull out the document now. I would just say generally, Your Honour, the fact that the Prosecution had the document in its possession really says nothing about its provenance in and of itself. I will inquire about the provenance of this particular document and report to the Chamber as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. In any event, what is suggested? Let's try and move on. It says -- just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. Let's try and do something for the witness. Do you know anything these conflicts alleged to have taken place on the three days before what happened in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember that at all, nor do I know about that. This is the first time that I'm hearing of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if it's true. One doesn't know. Yes. Let's move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Ramo Babajic? His father's name was Omer. He was from Glogova. Your own local from Glogova village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramo Babajic, yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that he was an extremist of the SDA party and that he participated in the attacks and killings of Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Including Magasici and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Nor did that man ever have any weapons or bear arms. I don't know if he's still alive. I'd like him to be so that he can come here and tell you. That man never -- no, come on. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That is what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stand by this. That is not true. No, no, not for Ramo either. Don't -- I'm not going to say what I don't know. Don't put things in like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about these events. I only have what I have on paper. 010807 is the number -- the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Now, the accused is putting some piece of paper he has got to you. There's no evidence where it comes from and no reliance can be placed on it at the moment, but deal with, if you would, with the allegations which he makes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's very short. Too short. I should like to be given at least a few more minutes for me to get through several of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know Ejub Golic, for example? His father's name was Mustafa, he was from Glogova also.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Golic Ejub. It wasn't Mustafa, his father's name was Latif.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, but do you know the man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he slit the throat of Marko Micic who had been detained, captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that he led operations against a number of villages in the Bratunac municipality, precisely that civilian from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. Because I had to receive medical treatment when I went to Potocari. I had to be treated for the state I was in. How do you expect me to know things like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The page is 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is the numbering of the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat the page number, please. It's not being interpreted. The microphones are down, Mr. Milosevic. We'll just have to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It is switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to adjourn. --- Break taken at 9.19 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've got ten minutes more. We'll sit for an hour and a half, we'll then take a 20-minute break and then sit for the rest of the time scheduled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear? Are you getting any translation? Can you hear the English on this channel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that my question wasn't recorded on the transcript so I'll repeat the question. This is it:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up this question of uniforms, Mr. 1701. Do you know that the entire Territorial Defence wore the same military uniforms, army uniforms, and that they had the uniforms in their own homes? That's where they kept them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that they had this uniform, the Yugoslav People's Army uniform. The Territorial Defence had quite a different -- quite different clothing. It was a little thinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that it was different from the JNA, but tell me this then: Do you happen to know that in the Bratunac municipality the entire Territorial Defence was, to all intents and purposes, all the command posts were held by Muslims? Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Sabit Mujkic, for example, who was commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of him. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I received this Territorial Defence clothing and handed it back, I didn't really know those people, nor did I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about the deputy commander for operative affairs and training, who was also a Muslim, and his name was Hadzic Dzemo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already told you I don't know any of those people. I worked in Drina, Srebrenica, in Sumarstvo. I really don't know any of the people working in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The one who issued the uniformed who was the logistics assistant, Becirevic Mevludin, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know any of them. I would just go there, sign my name, sign the receipt, get the clothing, get the uniform, and the same process when I took it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the commanders of the companies of Territorial Defence for your area, Konjevic Polje and Glogova and Ranca and all the other areas, Potcaus and Suha and all the rest of the places were all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I'm not going to ask you about that. What about this name, does that ring a bell: Avdic Senahid from Glogova, and his father's name was Idriz. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You do, right. Do you know that he is on the list of criminals that took part in the attack on Magasici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first I hear of it. The man was ill and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But for your record, it is on page 00678871. And did you mention Meho Cosic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't know that man nor did I mention him. He's not in my memory. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So -- but you know these other ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying I know them. I don't know him. I don't know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know Avdo Golic from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo Golic, yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he too is on the list of people who were killing and looting in Magasici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you say that? He was executed on the first -- on the 9th of May in Glogova. So don't make things up. He was executed at the same time when they shot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is 0085055. This is the page number.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can only ask me about the things I've decided to talk about. Don't ask me about things that didn't happen. Avdo was shot, executed. So we can see immediately that that is not correct. All these questions are not right. None of it is right. This question proves it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Esad Ibisevic from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Ibisevic Esad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he involved in killing, looting, burning houses in surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which villages? What do you mean? How can I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything his activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Esad Ibisevic was in Tuzla in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the war and everything, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in prison in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. He was in prison in Tuzla. So he was a criminal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I know what he was doing and why he was in prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he is here on the list of people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is not true. He wasn't there, nor did he participate. You see how you're asking me questions. There are no records. There's nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling the Court, not you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't say things that don't exist. It is page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is on page 00678857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this list that you're referring to, Mr. Milosevic? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received it from the opposite side, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what does it purport to be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a list of war criminals, consisting of more than 300 names who participated in the killing of Serbs in the area, and I asked him about this one from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. It may be that we're going to find out what it is, where this comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will look for these numbers that were just recently mentioned. Before we had the technical problem, Mr. Milosevic mentioned another document and I do have information for the Chamber on that. The number was -- the ERN number was 00017954 to 8085. The title of that document is "Memorandum on War Crimes and Crimes of Genocide in Eastern Bosnia Committed Against the Serbian Population from April 1992 to April 1993." That was prepared by the Yugoslav State Commission for War Crimes and Genocide and was submitted to the United Nations by the accused's own government. And I can -- the Prosecution cannot attest to anything about the reliability of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. It's something put forward by the Serbian side, allegations. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this document, Mr. Groome, 01025179, and I quoted page 01025 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. They're looking for that. You can tell us, if you can, what that document is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document provided by the Muslim side, not the Serb side, saying that these are activities by local paramilitary formations. That is not a document of the Serbian side, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I have that document here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Prosecution will try and find it. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You speak about the events that took place then. How far is the bus station from the shopping centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 250 metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say you saw Deronjic at the bus stop.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they were chasing me along the road, I didn't dare look left or right, he was standing there at the bus station with a couple of soldiers as we passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So passing by. So you went to the commercial centre and the Deronjic you mention as a person in a negative light, he was 250 metres away at the bus station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the bus station. Don't confuse me. I was saying at the bus station, together with two other men. And from there I was forced up there where the men were separated from the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, so that man wasn't present at all when these things were happening at the shopping centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How are you asking me these questions? I was telling you, as we were passing by, he was at the bus station together with maybe seven or ten people, and from there I was forced up to Mujo Osmanovic's house. After a while, he came again in a car. He just looked around, turned his car around, went back to the same spot at the bus station. Zaim Beganovic's house is there and Rabin Golic [phoen] told me that he held a meeting and he sent him home to get a rifle and he didn't have a rifle. And he told me this two days later, when he found me lying there. And he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're telling us about the return of weapons. You said that you surrendered weapons on the 5th of May and there were only three policemen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were three policemen at the gate. That's what I'm saying. But there were many of them along the macadam and asphalt roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but those policemen were both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when they had separated by then? The civilian police had all been separated. No one was working any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You're saying that you tried to escape together with Ramiz Cosic but the bullet hit Ramiz, he fell, and you were the only person who survived what was going on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right. Ramiz was not with me nor was I with him when he was killed. I heard later that Ramiz was killed as I went towards Srebrenica. That is not right. Don't ask me questions that are not right, that are quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm also talking about that. Don't say that. The man asked me about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In point 31, you say -- I'm not asking you things that you didn't say. In paragraph 31, you say what I have just asked you. "Serb soldiers told us to run towards the wood," and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're confusing me. You're mixing up things that happened maybe 15 or 20 days later when the man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But didn't you say a moment ago that you didn't see Ramiz being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were told that Ramiz was killed, and you didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father told me when he found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. That's why I'm asking you. You say here: "I saw the head of Ramiz Cosic being blown off."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ramiz Cosic. Because he was on my right side. You're mixing up Ramiz Cosic and Ramiz Gerovic. These are two different things for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must bring this to a close. You can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard to select two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the Muslim army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I don't know exactly when, I don't know the date. I joined -- I couldn't walk, I couldn't do anything. I was peeling potatoes so I could get food to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many times this Magasici was attacked by Muslim forces, and that the persons who committed crimes have been identified; that is, Osmanovic, Junuz, Meho from Magasici; Osmanovic Saban; Hasanovic Camil [phoen]; Carmin Adica [phoen]; Naket Nasir [phoen]; Babjic Ramo [phoen]; Smajlovic Rahiden [phoen]; Osmanovic Hajrudin. They have all been identified for attacking and killing Serbian civilians, all civilians in Magasici that you have spoken about. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you some questions about the 9th of May. And on that day, some of the people who were attacking the area had masks on and others did not. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all had masks over their faces, and I couldn't see any one of them without a mask when the village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at a statement you made to the Prosecution on the 2nd of March of last year, and in that statement you say: "The Serbs were mostly wearing masks, but some were not." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it. I only saw Deronjic who didn't have a mask on his face. As for the others, they all were masked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And after you've said that some of the Serbs were not wearing masks, you name some people from the Glogova district whom you recognised from the 9th of May, and you knew they were Serbs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean later on when I saw Milo Riba and the others, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right. On the 9th of May --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They weren't attacking anyone. They were not insulting anyone or anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw someone you knew as Milo Riba, who used to have a private truck, but he was wearing a --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- SMB uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all in SMB uniforms, each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw Zaric Milan. He was a house painter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw Radic Gojko. He was a driver.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the Drina company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw Pero, who was a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he was in another group. He wasn't with them, those that had masks over their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Don't worry where people were. I'm just asking you about those you describe as the attackers on the 9th of May. It doesn't matter what they were doing, it's just who they were. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Those men didn't have masks over their faces. They didn't attack anyone, they didn't say anything to anyone. I was just being forced up there with my dear mother. That's all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But they had uniforms on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army. All, each and every one of them. Let's not talk about uniforms. All those soldiers were wearing the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you knew those people, those names I've given you, were not in the army. They were neighbours of yours. They were local people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All neighbours. I knew them. I knew that they weren't officers. I never saw them in uniform before. Milo Riba helped me a lot when I was building my house. It is hard to imagine that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic you describe as being a leader of the attackers at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was the leader. I can't say that. I didn't know that he was a leader nor what he was doing. I just saw him there when we were being executed. When we carried the bodies and came back for the second group, he again came wearing a SMB officer's uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army and a beret on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw Deronjic giving orders on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He wasn't issuing any orders. He was just standing still and observing things. He didn't speak a word, that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had he given orders to you before the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't issuing orders at all. He just came. He held two meetings, as far as I can remember, that's all, that we shouldn't panic, that nothing would happen, that we should surrender our weapons, that our weapons would be returned to us after they had been checked, and that was all. He didn't say anything more to us. That was it. At least, I don't remember while I was there. Now, later on, whether he came and spoke to the president of the local community, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: However, on the 9th of May when you first saw Deronjic, he was wearing civilian clothes when you first saw him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then he put on a uniform later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later. I saw him in uniform when we were down there after the execution. When we were carrying the bodies and when we came back for the second group, he was wearing a SMB officer's uniform with a beret on his head. He didn't say anything to anyone. He was just standing at attention and watching people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if people -- if it was common in your area for people to keep their old army uniforms if they'd be in the TO or if they had been in the regular army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You had to hand it in immediately. If you don't hand it in, the police would chase you around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time, lots of people were wearing old JNA uniforms, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't notice anything or observe it. Who would wear it? Only these soldiers that I saw. I couldn't see anyone else. And I didn't know who they were. They had socks over their heads. How could I recognise them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Later on, you joined the BH army as a cook; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long did you work for the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three months after Srebrenica fell. I peeled potatoes. I couldn't do much. My hands hurt, my back; I wasn't in good health, I wasn't fit. My hand is still not all right. I had to work a little so I would get aid to be able to feed my family. There were five with me that I had to look after, though I wasn't really able to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But for how long did you work for that army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About five months. Not more, I'm sure. After Srebrenica fell, that is when I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions. One other matter to help over the names that were given. I don't know if Mr. Groome has been able to see document 00799571 in English. It's a list on the same subject, and it's one that I was able to pick up. I don't know if that helps the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll look at that document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of your testimony over the last two days you've mentioned two people by the name of Ramiz. The person with the name Ramiz who was next to you at the river when you were shot at and Ramiz was killed, what was his last name? Give us his full name, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cosic Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other Ramiz that you mentioned in your testimony, Ramiz Gerovic, you were not personally present --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other Ramiz, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were not personally present when he was killed, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kay has asked you about the names of four men who you mentioned in your statement as people that you recognised. Can you tell the Chamber in a sentence or two the circumstances under which you saw those four men on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milo Riba and the others. You're referring to them, are you? Is that what you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Without going into great detail, can you just briefly describe how it was you came to see those men and recognise those men, and what you saw them doing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was being herded along the asphalt. They were on the right-hand side in front of the school, and that is how I recognised them. They came to the road, they were quiet, they didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we didn't understand what the witness say. He used a word "okahani" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to repeat the last portion of your answer. The interpreters had a bit of trouble hearing it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was going along the road, on the right-hand side -- I was going on the right-hand side, and to the right of the schoolyard they were going, and they reached the asphalt road, and we were going on with women. There were lots of us. And they stopped there and were observing us. They didn't say anything at all. Ah, they were very sad. They looked sad, as if they were about to cry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there's been a great deal of discussion about uniforms and whether they were old or new and whether people were allowed to keep them after they left the service of the JNA. The question I have for you is: You've mentioned seeing a number of tanks, a number of armoured personnel carriers in the town at the time of the attack. My question is: Prior to April of 1992, did you see these vehicles, these tanks, these armoured personnel carriers, in the town of Bratunac or in Glogova prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see those vehicles in Bratunac in front of the fountain -- Fontana, parked there, and down there, close to the hospital or health centre. That is where those vehicles were. There were lots of troops. They were all wearing JNA clothing with light machine-guns. At the department store, there was a soldier on every corner and a woman with him. And all their weapons were on the ready. And that is how I passed. I didn't go back to Bratunac again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Chamber, what is the earliest point in time that you can recall seeing this level of military machinery in the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when I went to Bratunac, I saw them. That's it. I went to report to my company, right behind the police station. That is where my company was. I went to the company to see what they wanted of me, and that's when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As far as you could tell, the tanks, the armoured personnel carriers, were they vehicles belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who else could they belong to? They couldn't belong to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Your Honour, just an observation regarding a number of documents that have been used in the cross-examination. I have been able to get details of some of them, just awaiting details on others. But many -- the other documents that the -- Mr. Milosevic referred to was a document. All I can find out about it was that it was submitted by an individual. The general rule or general policy of the Office of the Prosecutor is that it has accepted reports and submissions by parties, and has used them as an investigative tool to identify crimes that the Prosecutor should investigate. It's never been the Prosecution's position that these documents themselves or these reports prepared by individuals or individual groups have any great evidential value in and of themselves. They're just matters to be further investigated by the office. They've just been provided to the accused and the amici as part of our obligations under discovery of Rule 66 and 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In relation to this witness, various statements were referred to, and it is clear, I think, that they should probably be exhibited. These are the statements which he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is Your Honour thinking about the OTP statement as well as the earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution would have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be done. It may be that you could get Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us copies of those statements. We've got them already. We'll get the next -- since the Prosecution -- we'll have the next Prosecution number, I think might be as convenient as anything.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 431, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Witness B-1701, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask, with respect to those exhibits, that they be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness has the pleasure of protection. Very little of her evidence will be the subject of an application for private session, and I'll turn to that in just a second. But first, in light of the problems this morning, does the Chamber still want to deal with administrative matters in the third session or, given the real priority of ensuring that this witness is finished before the long Easter break, might it be preferable to put administration back to the end of her evidence tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that. And so that everyone knows the position, I might not have made myself clear yesterday when I was addressing you on the length of submissions from the Prosecution. What I have in mind is that we should begin with the 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then the Foca transcript witnesses, and only finally get on to the matters as far as time and disclosure are concerned. If we deal with them in that way, at least we will deal with those matters which we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. And the other matters are the subject of written motions in any event. Before the witness comes in, and this may be a policy the Court would prefer with all witnesses where there is any application for private session, I identify the limited amount of material that she would want in private session. Are we presently in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-129 - paragraph 1 and 2, Your Honours - is it right that you worked in 1993 for the Party of Serbian Unity not out of political affiliation but because it was a well-paid job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was your work initially limited to election matters, there being no war activities concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have contact with the man Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During the election campaign, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there also some members of his Tigers unit that worked in the same office as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because most of them who were in the Serbian Volunteer Guards during the election campaign were given different things to do within the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1994, did you start to work at the headquarters of the SSJ and SDG in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give the expansion of both those titles? SSJ being?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: SSJ is the Party of Serbian Unity. And the SDG is the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Also known as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your work bring you into regular and close contact with Arkan, his office being one floor removed from yours but he tasking you -- giving you tasks as long as -- as well as many other people every day, or several other people every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would see him every day, and most of the day he would spend at the headquarters of the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guards. So we often saw each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraph 6. Did you, perhaps along with others, take phone calls for Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he have a secretary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a secretary, his own personal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was the placing and receiving of calls done by you and others through that secretary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I myself would answer the phone, the incoming telephone calls, and sometimes it would be his secretary and then she would pass the line on to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you keep a diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was my diary of daily duties, my agenda for today, what duties I had on each particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first extract from your diary we'll look at is tab 2 of Exhibit 432, please. It will come up on your screen if it's not there already. What, as a matter of fact, is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the former commander of the -- the late commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, Zeljko Raznjatovic, which I used when I had to write a letter in his name, an answer, a response to somebody or give approval for something, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Exhibit 391, tab 7, please. The exhibit has already been looked at. What do you see on the bottom right-hand part of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see there is the signature of the commander, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. And he signed that in Erdut, which means that it is the same signature except for the fact that this is written in his own hand, his own personal signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraph 10. On what date was the group known as the Tigers established and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group was established -- the date at which the Serbian National Guard was formed is taken to be the 11th of October, 1990. And the place of its establishment, the establishment of the guards, is the monastery of Pokajnica, a monastery near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that date, the 11th of October, celebrated every year since then, a certain number of years, as the date of the anniversary of the foundation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was celebrated every year. Sometimes the celebrations would be held in Erdut and sometimes in the monastery of the Pokajnica itself, depending on where the guards were at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many men initially took the oath appropriate to that group, and then name some of those initial ones that you can now recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about ten of them. However -- or, rather, first of all there was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Then there was Nebojsa Djordjevic, nicknamed Suca. Then there was Nenad Markovic, also known as Sicko. Sasa Pavlovic, also known as Crvko; and Dragan Petrovic, also known as Kajman; and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Tab 3, please, of Exhibit 432 is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph we see Nebojsa Djordjevic, as known as Suca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps it can go on the overhead projector as it hasn't found it's way into the computerised system. I won't take time on it. We'll come back to the photograph in a minute when the system is back in its normal operation. Can we turn then to tab 4, which again I think is not on the computerised system. The Chamber may wish to look at that. Can you tell us, please, Witness B-129, what this list is and how it's been composed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list contains the names of the members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards. Then we have the names of the Red Berets. When I say "Red Berets," I mean the special unit of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you compose this list yourself? Was it provided to you? Explain, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I compiled the list myself with the names of the people that I would see or hear about during my work in the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guards, so when I was going about my daily duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will see on the first sheet names with which it will perhaps already be familiar in part, such as -- looking at the third column, Veliki Rambo, and further down, Mali Rambo. Over the page, third entry, Zika Crnogorac; fourth from the bottom, Legija. Next sheet, three up from the bottom, Kajman, to whom there will be further reference. Arkan himself at the bottom. And then on the last -- the next sheet, four up from the bottom, Frenki. And on the last sheet, three up from the bottom, Legija. I'm alerted by -- oh, yes. I'm invited to draw your attention on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with that Legija name. It hasn't been clear, but it appears he's got two names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, Witness B-129, with the nickname Legija. To whom was that associated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legija relates to Milorad Ulemek or Milorad Lukovic. His real surname was Ulemek, however, as he had fled from the Foreign Legion during 1994, on the 3rd of September, in fact, when he married, he took his wife's surname, which was Lukovic. So it's one and the same person but he goes by two different surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're now looking at the photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're now looking at a photograph, Witness B-129. Please tell us who is shown.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph we see Nebojsa Djorjevic, nicknamed Suca, one of the founders of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to identify any of the others in the background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Guard seems to have been described as a Volunteer Guard but also as the National Guard. Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This Guard was only known as the Serbian Volunteer Guard, the SDG, or the Tigers. The Srpska Dobrovojacka Garda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So any reference to the National Guard is to something else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that there may be problems with the playing of the intercepts which will mean we will have to return to those later. I'll just check with the technical booth whether there is a problem. And, Your Honour, while we're waiting for information on the state of the technical booth or its ability to deal with the intercepts, I'm also asked to draw to your attention on that last tab, the list, on page 1, the fifth entry, which is Raja Bozovic, is a name that's going to be referred to. On the third sheet, the third entry, Vasa Mijovic; the 6th entry, Sasa Pavlovic. And on the next sheet, in the middle of the page, Mladen Sarac, and then the two Ulemeks that we've already dealt with. Apparently, Your Honour, there is no audio coming out of the intercepts so that we hope that can be remedied over the break. And although it will enforce some discontinuity on the evidence, I'm sure that we can fit those intercepts in when we come to them at a later stage. In your summary, therefore, if you'd be good enough to go to paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Having looked at the list we have, Witness B-129, Crvko and Sicko, can you tell us a little bit about them, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sicko and Crvko, in addition to being the founders of the Guards Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were wounded in 1991 in Tenja, which is Eastern Slavonia. After that, they were not able to go to the front any more so that their duties linked to the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guard, was at the headquarters in Ljutice Bogdana street, number 1. And I would meet them on a daily basis. I would come in to them. And Sicko was in charge of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they speak to you of their experiences with the Tigers on operational duty; and if so, where did they tell you that they had been engaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They spoke about all the operations in Eastern Slavonia in 1991. They did not speak about how the operations evolved themselves, but they said where they were, such as Tenja, Borovo Selo, Mirkovci, the Tenski Antunovac, and all the smaller places in Eastern Slavonia, with the exception of Vukovar. They would always say that the Guard was never in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything about activities in Bosnia or the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They spoke about that too, about Bosnia, but they spoke about Bosnia and Krajina as did Arkan and some of the other members who happened to be at the headquarters of the SDG. They would also talk about Bijeljina, Zvornik, Brcko. That was in the course of 1992. And Krajina in January and February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What detail did they provide you of what they'd done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Bijeljina is concerned, Arkan himself said he had gone at the invitation of Biljana Plavsic to assist the Serb people in Republika Srpska and that their assignment was to disarm the Muslims, especially in the village of Janja, which is near Bijeljina, next to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is dealt with at paragraph 62, but I take it now for speed. When he told you that, did he say who was in charge of the Bijeljina operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say who was in charge, but he did say that he defended Bijeljina with Mauzer, that is to say Major Mauzer, who was also at the beginning in the Serbian Democratic -- in the Serbian Volunteer Guard, the SDG, and then he went on to for the Panther unit later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there somebody called Cobe, I think it's Cobe, first name Slobodan whose last name wasn't known but his code name was Cobe, who was also involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In all those operations, he was in them all, and later on he was in Brcko or, rather, Celici which is a place near Brcko where Cobe was wounded. And he talked about these operations because he worked in a bakery, so we bumped into each other every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And since you've already told us about involvement in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Brcko as described by Arkan and others - paragraph 61 - on whose orders, as you were informed, were the Tigers working when they went to these various places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please? I don't think I understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My mistake. These early operations in Bijeljina, Zvornik and Brcko, who gave the order that they should go and work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan would always say that without orders from the DB, the state security, the Tigers were not deployed anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that the intercepts are now available to us. Can we go back, then, to paragraph 13. There are a couple of intercepts to play, and although sometimes we deal with it by transcripts alone, I think the total of somewhere up to about nine minutes may be worth having in full on this occasion. If we decide that it's not or it seems to be unduly wearisome, we can proceed by way of the transcript. The first intercept is to be found transcribed at your tab 5, and I'd ask the witness to have before her a transcript in whichever language she finds most convenient, but probably the B/C/S, and we'll follow it in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Voiceover] B: Good morning. Good morning, Biljana Plavsic speaking. Is Zeljko there, please? X: He's not here, Mr. Rus is here. Will he do? B: Yes. Put him through, please. R: Hello. B: Good morning. R: Good morning. My great respect, ma'am. Rus speaking. B: How are you? R: The commander's bat man. B: I know, I know. R: I'm just getting ready to attend the raising of the flag. B: Oh, the raising of the flag. I won't keep you long. R: No, no, not at all. Please, what can I do for you? B: I just wanted to ask, Zeljko is not around, is he? R: Well, you know what? I would be very much obliged if you could tell me when you'd like to call again so that I would know to call him. B: You know why I am -- R: He was away -- B: Never mind, then. I'll tell you what it's about. I returned to my base where I come from. But I still haven't reached my house because a small section is blocked. But I wanted just to ask him in principle, if there was a call to come here, would that be possible? R: Listen, ma'am, I don't have enough authority to speak on his behalf. B: I know, of course. R: But I'll make sure that he gets your message immediately. B: Yes. Pass it on. And when I get to my flat, I'll -- R: Call him? B: Yes. But then I won't ask him this. I will only ask will you bring those goods, if possible. R: Of course, of course. B: Is that right? R: Of course. Listen, ma'am, if it's possible for you to call in about two hours. It's 8.00 now. If you could call in about two hours, I'll tell him. B: All right. R: In about an hour. B: All right, all right. R: I hope it's not too much to ask. B: All right. R: I am really sorry that the situation is as it is. He's really -- you know, he always attends the raising of the flag but he went to bed very late. B: All right. Tell me, what's it like in Zvornik? Can you tell me that? R: Excuse me? B: What's it like in Zvornik? Has Pejo gone there? R: Well, I don't know. He should go there as well. The situation, the whole situation, since there are all kinds of rumours. He must be here, the poor fellow. He really doesn't have time for everything and for himself. I'll convey to him all that. B: All right. If I call from another phone, then I'll just ask whether he can deliver those things to me so we know in principle if he can. And then we should discuss it. R: Fine. B: All right. Say hello to him, and thank you. R: Thank you. And it was a honour talking to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-129, are you able to recognise the voice of the man speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Rus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Full name was Vladimir Homa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladimir Homa, Rus. He was a major by rank. He was killed in 1993 at Celici near Brcko. He was very close to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To whom Mrs. Plavsic was clearly seeking to speak. The reference to raising of the flag twice and the fact that Arkan would attend the raising of the flag identifies Rus as being where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Erdut. In Erdut, every morning the flag was raised, and in the evening it was lowered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But elsewhere was it possible -- at other locations of the Tigers, was it possible to raise a flag or was it only at Erdut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can see the nature of the inquiries that Mrs. Plavsic was making. Are you able to assist one way or another with the goods that she's referring to when she says, "I'll ask that you bring those goods"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The reference on the second page to Pejo, who is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference is to Marko Pejic, also known as Pejo. He was a general by rank in the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and he participated in operations in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, I think, on this, I asked you whether you recognised the voice, but I must just check. Do you recognise the voice or is it simply that you know the man Rus and from the context of the transcript can say who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the transcript, I can conclude that it is the -- Rus speaking, because I did not have occasion to meet Rus. But Arkan frequently spoke about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm reminded by Ms. Wee that it's possible for you to follow the transcripts on the screen under the system, if you wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That intercept, of course, is subject to a ruling on admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There then comes tab 6, which is two transcripts. Transcripts of two intercepts. If we can play the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Voiceover] L: Captain Legija speaking. I'm calling from Sarajevo. X: Well, where have you been? L: Is 99 there? X: 99 is sleeping, having a little rest. L: When will he get up? X: I don't know. Give me your number. You should be returning. L: Yes. X: I know that, too. Ljubinko called to see how you could return. Basically, you have to return somehow. L: I know. That's why I'm calling. X: I'm glad. L: We feel like crying over here. Tell 99 that I will call in two hours. X: That you will call in two hours? So around quarter to 8.00? Phone about 1900 or a quarter past. I think he has something to attend to at 1930 hours. L: All right. X: Are you all okay? L: Yes, apart from two men. X: Are they in Pale? L: Yes. X: Say hello to Bojovic. L: Bye.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise either or both of those voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Legija is Milorad Lukovic or Ulemek, because in 1992 he had the rank of captain and I recognise his voice. "99" is the wartime code for Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. And the female voice is of that Snezana Kalinic who was the personal secretary of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. And she left the headquarters in March 1994. Ljubinko, the man that is mentioned as Ljubinko, is Ljubinko Jevtic, a general by rank in the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that on this intercept we have Captain Legija from Sarajevo seeking to contact Arkan, known as 99, through his secretary, with the conversation we see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second conversation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Voiceover] L: Hello, Commander. Hello, Commander. A: Fire away, Legija. L: I just wanted to ask you about the matter that Bojke called you about this morning. A: Well, we can't find the stinkers anywhere. L: All right, but since he told me to call you. A: Yes. Tell me that we haven't yet found the stinkers for that. L: All right. I'll try something from here. A: It would be good if they could do something from there. But what was it? L: Did Bojke explain things this morning? A: Yes. L: That's how it is. We cannot stand still. There's nothing we can do. This place is full of war profiteers. It's as if someone went to Belgrade now and went to Badza and told him you are this and you are that. That's how it is here. A: Yes, yes. L: They look at us now as if we had fallen from the sky. A certain Mladic has now appeared. I quarreled with him up there today. A: What happened with Mladic? L: We stopped 7.200 refugees. We stopped them. I suggested that Mladic exchange them for the barracks over there. They said all right, all right. He called Panic and Panic said that they should be released but that we were a humane people, et cetera. When they said that, Mladic said that I should see about it with my men. A: What did he say? L: That I should see with my men. I told him I have done my job and the fact that you are playing at diplomacy with them over the phone and they have screwed you again, that's not my job, and I left. Later, he called me again, saying we should have a civilised discussion and should not quarrel. I then explained everything to him. But then again, these people here, this command up here, they are not registering us. They refuse to accept who we are and what we are. I don't want to quarrel any longer. They will soon arrest me. A: Well, if that is how it is, what are you doing there? They really are stinkers. L: I made thousands of suggestions and tried thousands of other ways to include these people here, but it was no use. We haven't been in action for two days now because I do not want to go into action and lose one man every day for no reason, and we're still at a standstill. It's terribly stupid. I don't know. This Karadzic guy is up there too. They all embrace those Muslims. They are negotiating with them. I captured 7.200 people for them. I said Fikret Abdic too that they are Serbs from these -- they cut the throats of about 200 Serbs. Tell them that these are the Serbs who survived and that they stopped them, that because of that slaughter, they are looking for -- that they stopped that convoy and are asking for the release of all the soldiers from the barracks. They negotiated, and these people screwed them again. A: Another betrayal, then. L: They should have released these soldiers at 8.00 this morning, but when the convoy left the barracks, Juka's men -- there's someone called Juka, some guy who is the leader of the Green Berets. He started shooting at them and they turned back. All of our men were afraid and decided to let them go. A: Damn them. L: I was barely able to persuade Mladic to retain the convoy because for as long as the convoy is in your hands, their side will not attack. He then started blathering again. I haven't got the patience to quarrel with them here. They all quarrel about who will be in command, and no one wants a discussion on how to attack and launch an offensive to finally bring about the fall of Sarajevo. I have spoken to Sulc and Bajke, and I think the best solution is to return there. A: That would be best. See if you can take a helicopter from there. L: I'll try with this main colonel. A: See what you can do. L: All right, bye. A: Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you've dealt with this tape, this intercept, we'll take a break, the tape's got to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you recognise their voices?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need to break right now, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-129, reviewing what is the second part of tab 6 of Exhibit 432, a transcript of the video we most -- of the intercept we most recently heard, are you able to recognise both voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are Legija, Milorad Lukovic or Milorad Ulemek. And the second voice was the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At an early part of the transcript we see two references to the "stinkers." Was that a term that may have other meanings but was used by them in conversation to mean something in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commander used that expression, he had in mind the members of the DB, state security, or members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We see it used later in a context which may make it hard. This is on the second page for the Court. After a long answer by Legija where there's an answer which goes: "Well, if that's how it is -- if that's how it is, what are you doing there? They really are stinkers." Can this same word mean something else, or in their context would -- or in their use would it always mean the DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it meant that it referred to members of the DB. But in this context, it can also mean something else. So the expression itself wasn't always used to refer to the DB members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. It's simply -- it can be simply a bad word, a term of abuse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we look at the beginning of the transcript, the very first substantive observation by Legija, he speaks about somebody called Bojke. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bojke was in fact an officer, and his surname was Bojovic. I myself never met him, but Snezana Kalinic, the secretary, told me that he was an officer of the Serbian Volunteer Guard during the operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Finally, on particular matters of the transcript, at the end of the transcript, the second page, six lines up from the bottom there's a reference to Legija having spoken to Sulc and Bajke, and our interpreters in the English booth did read out the word "Sulc." Do you have a view as to whether it should be Sulc or whether it should be someone else or can't you assist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood it, as I understood Legija in that particular conversation, what it should be is Suca. Suca and Bojke.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you say it should be that, is that from the context you say it should be that or from what you were able to hear of the intercept itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I heard in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then finally because we've the content in mind, I think the position is you're not able to give any particular overall context for this intercept; is that right? You can't interpret it for us beyond what it says itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your knowledge of the Tigers' involvement in and around Sarajevo being what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It referred just to the Treskavica operation, Treskavica 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps it's convenient to pick up tab 7 straight away as we've had the first use of a number for Arkan, number 99. Do you produce as our tab 7 a chart which contains, in a slightly redacted form, a number of the call-signs that were in use by the Tigers or the SDG in the time that you were working for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I compiled this list myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we can see the sign 66 for Mihajlo Ulemek, 99 for Arkan, Tiger-1 for Legija, and so on. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I come to a number of particular topics. Special Tigers. Tell us about them in a sentence or so, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Special Tigers or Super Tigers were formed in 1993, while the first camp in Erdut was in existence. And their commander was Milorad Lukovic, Legija. And that particular unit was supposed to be a sort of special unit within the frameworks of the Serbian Democratic Guard -- I'm sorry, Serbian Volunteer Guard. And some of their members provided security. When I say provided security, what I mean is they worked as bodyguards for certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When the Tigers were on operation, was a military police unit created? If so, to what purpose and effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always when the guard was in the field, on the ground, within the frameworks of the SDG a unit was set up of the military police, which was assigned to members of the SDG. It was made up of their members. And the purpose for forming that particular unit was to prevent the SDG members from looting and from mistreating the civilian population, from getting drunk and so on. So to act in any way contrary to the code of conduct of the SDG.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were those military units ad hoc being disbanded when the action was terminated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military police would be disbanded after every SDG operation came to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Arkan's attitude to prisoners, please. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan would always say, during the time that I was in the Serbian Volunteer Guard, that they did not have prisoners. But in the course of 1991 and 1992, for example, there was a man who was put in charge of exchanging prisoners of war, and his name was Vojkan Djurkovic. We referred to him as Voja Bijeljina because he was from Bijeljina. I know about that because that man was later on engaged in the work of the party of democratic unity, Serbian Democratic Unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was your understanding of Arkan's phrase that he did not or they did not have prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and all the rest understood this as meaning that those prisoners of war were in fact killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
