utterances.text: Paragraph 24. Membership of the SDG and its numbers. We're going to hear about the opening of the second Erdut camp in 1995, and about that time, how many, roughly, Tigers were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to? Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1995, there were about 100 Tigers, but all of them at that particular period were in Velika Kladusa, engaged in a secret operation which was put into effect together with the DB of the Republic of Serbia under the leadership of Radojica Bozovic, nicknamed Raja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. I'm just concerned about numbers. You've told us about how many, roughly, took the oath at the beginning. Did the numbers of Tigers rise and fall over time or did they just go up or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the total number of people by 1995 was approximately how many do you say, how many Tigers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're thinking about the period during the summer of 1995 after the operation, after the Storm operation in Krajina at the end of August, if we don't count those who were forcibly mobilised, the population who was forcibly mobilised, in the guard in Erdut there were about 1.000 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On joining, did volunteers have to fill in a form and be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any check done on criminal records?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would conduct an interview with them. And there was a form on which we would note down their basic credentials, and then we would talk to them ourselves and we would try not to recruit people which we would see straight away were drug addicts or had other psychological problems. And as to whether some of them had criminal records with the police, we didn't have the ability to check that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Apart from yourself and others, was the man Sicko involved in the selection of new members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We've dealt with the numbers, the recruitment. The disbanding of the Tigers, when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second time. No, sorry. Well, in March or April of 1996 were they disbanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the end of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. March or April 1996 was the date when they left the camp in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And at that stage, did at least two of their members join another unit in the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Milorad Lukovic, Legija, and Nenad Bujosevic, nicknamed Big Rambo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The unit they joined was called what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit was called the Red Berets of the state security of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The JSO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We've dealt with call-signs. Paragraph 28 just, though, to complete it. You've produced the chart that you have of call-signs. Were those call-signs or some of them at any event subject to change during operations, for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These signs, the ones which I have before me, did not change. The only thing is -- the only signs that were changed were the signs which they used in the field, amongst themselves. So they used it for radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when they were operational, did the Tigers carry lists of codes with them for communication by radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was part of their equipment. Every one of them, on their left hand above the elbow, would have a piece of plastic attached to their arms, and they have a partition where the code is introduced and extracted. So whenever they would go into an operation of any kind, the officer leading them would assign them new codes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When they went on operations, what did the Tigers have to do with their own personal, genuine identification documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ID cards would be left either at the headquarters in Belgrade, they would leave them behind, and afterwards -- and they could do this in Erdut, too, at the Erdut headquarters once the Erdut centre was opened up again. We would then take those ID cards of theirs and their personal belongings, pack them all up, place them in envelopes with their names written up on them and we'd store them in a cupboard, and they would be given separate membership cards of the Serb Volunteer Guard with just their names on them and their photograph and blood type.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What uniforms did the Tigers have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tigers had two types of uniform; one was green camouflage, the type of uniform was the NATO type of uniform. And other type of uniform was a black one, and that one was used for night operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What headgear did they use with either of these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the green uniforms, the officers wore the red beret, whereas the rank and file, the ordinary soldiers, would wear green caps. But both of them had the insignia the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guard, on them. However, when they used the black uniforms, they would have the Balaclava hats -- socks on their heads, known as Fantomka, the phantom mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The unit's shoulder patch, did that have a picture of a tiger on it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you please repeat it into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the shoulder patch have a picture of a Tiger on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When they were on operations in Treskavica and Velika Kladusa, what if any patches did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that in Treskavica and Velika Kladusa they didn't have the insignia of the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guard, because they were told prior to leaving that they weren't allowed to use those. That means that in Velika Kladusa, what they had was insignia used by the army of Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us a little about discipline. What sanctions for breach of the code were imposed? For example, if a Tiger was caught drinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The punishment for drinking was the most rigorous. It was 100 lashes on the backside. But everyone in the Erdut camp would watch this, even those who just happened to be there, happened to be visiting. And even I myself witnessed this on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Arkan's expressed views on the unfolding of events there, what were his views about Republika Srpska and the RSK and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan was in favour of defending the Serbs in the RS and the RSK, but he was also in favour of keeping those territories that had been captured at that time. And I'm talking about the period I was there in 1994 and 1995, and not to go on to win over new territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you aware of the things he said in October 1993 at the foundation of his party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean about the Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina or do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not satisfied with the policy being waged at the time in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in the Republic of Serbia, because he considered that all Serbs should unite but that that unification did not mean trouble for the other peoples living on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before the war, for whom had Arkan worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he worked for the DB, the state security of the then Yugoslavia, although -- actually, the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you hear this from him or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From him -- I never heard this from him personally, but I heard it from a person whose nickname was Kale. And she worked in an agency for the security of Delije. Kale would often speak about that, that the two of them worked together. And this could be deduced from the respect that the late commander had towards Kale.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not "she," "he."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Serbian DB: To what extent were the Tigers dependant on support, permission or authority of the Serbian DB for what they did? What did Arkan say about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security, the DB, whenever it didn't have enough men for the front, it would take some of the members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. Or if they didn't have enough men to take up a certain position, then they would engage members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. The most important thing in this respect is that the Guard could do nothing on its own, nothing without permission from the DB of Serbia. And as far as the frontline goes, they did as best they could there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that, for example, when they were on operations in Eastern Slavonia in 1991, or in Bosnia in the following year, as what or in what capacity did the Tigers go on operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the capacity of the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia or, rather, the DB of Serbia, state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Contacts between Frenki and Arkan, did they happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With what sort of frequency, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When operations were under way, that is to say when the Guard was in Velika Kladusa and Treskavica during the Banja Luka operation, those contacts or telephone conversations were at least twice a week, twice weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What methods of calling Frenki were available to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two telephone numbers. One telephone number was linked to his office, that is to say was to his secretary, Sladjana. And the other number was a duty number of the state security of the Republic of Serbia. At the beginning, we would just have to give the code, and that was Pauk, meaning "spider." And this related to the Pauk operation in Velika Kladusa. However, several months later, a couple of months later, it would be enough for us to say where we were calling from and then we would be linked to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Tab 8 of Exhibit 432 on the screen or available in hard copy. Does this show the two telephone numbers you've been speaking of, and does it come from your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The first number, telephone number, is the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. duty officer, and the second telephone number is Frenki's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Border crossings next. When it was necessary to organise crossing of equipment, vehicles, people into Republika Srpska, what was done? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When something needed to cross via Raca, this would usually happen at night, because at that border crossing, usually there was UN control. I just needed to announce the vehicle, that is the licence plates, the number of the licence plates, and nothing more than that. They were not interested in what was inside or who was inside. It was sufficient for me to tell them the licence plate numbers or, that is, the word of the Serbian Volunteer Guard was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Frenki's secretary Sladjana, as you've told us, how often did you speak to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During an operation, two or three times a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if anything, did she tell you about the chains of command that affected Frenki; to whom he responded, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She always said that Frenki was in charge of the unit for special operations and that he could decide about certain things but that, without the approval of Jovica Stanisic, he could not take any decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that for example, Velika Kladusa, if you were informed or if you were told things from which you had an understanding, where did the authority for that come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the organisation of the Tigers for Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November 1994, Arkan told me that I should call up men on a certain list. At that point in time, I didn't know why. After calling these men up, Arkan told me that Frenki had been asking for men to reinforce his units in Velika Kladusa. So that on the 4th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Pausing there --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the first group left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Pausing there. Perhaps my error, but we'll come back to it. The operation itself, the overall operation, would that be something, as you understood it, within the authority of Frenki or would that have required the approval or instruction of Stanisic, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty, but Frenki was also on the ground in Velika Kladusa so that Jovica Stanisic should have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we turn from the topic of your conversation with Sladjana, Frenki's secretary, did she say anything about the accused Milosevic in this trial and his relationship to either Stanisic or Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What meetings, if any, did -- or did you become aware of between Arkan and Frenki, and who went to see whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the meetings during the Velika Kladusa operation, though they were less frequent then. But more frequent meetings were held during the Banja Luka operation, because they were afraid that Banja Luka would fall into the hands of the enemy. So that Arkan frequently went to see Frenki during that period of time. Arkan always went to see Frenki. I saw Frenki only once, and that was very early in the morning in front of our headquarters at the parking space.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned already - paragraph 46 - that when operational, the Tigers were -- went as reserve members of the Serbian DB. Did they actually get DB identification cards or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They kept their own over there. I mean, those of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened when Tigers were wounded so far as cards, medical cards, and their reserve membership of the DB is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone was seriously wounded, he would be admitted at the VMA, that is the medical academy hospital, or a civilian hospital and there would be no problems. But there would be problems for subsequent treatment. In that case, I would call up Sladjana, and I would send her the medical card, the health card of the wounded combatant which she would stamp with the stamp of the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia, which means that they would cover the expenses of his medical insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The camp at Erdut was reopened in 1995. What vehicle licence plates was Arkan able to use at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security gave him licence plates which are identical with those used by the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was he able to put them on and off vehicles as necessary or as useful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were those plates used for the transport of weapons, and if so, did it have the effect of avoiding interference by the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But when talking about weapons, I am referring only to pistols, because the only things that went from Belgrade to Erdut during operations were pistols or uniforms, because other weapons were given to them in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were Vukovar and Belgrade licence plates also available at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because our vehicles had the mark of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the tiger on the front part of the vehicle so that the regular police - and I am thinking of the regular police force - did not dare to stop those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the reopening of the Erdut training centre, what was the telephone connection between the Belgrade headquarters and Erdut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the headquarters in Belgrade and Erdut, there were a couple of telephone lines. A couple of them had the code number had to be dialed, but there was one line that had the same number as the Belgrade telephone numbers so that we didn't have to dial the area code for Erdut. Plus we had a radio station, a radio transmitter whereby we were directly linked to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And whose approval was required or what body's approval was required for this radio station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our rules and laws, by the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Moving on to 1996, were you contacted, along with others, by Frenki's secretary at the time when the Tigers had now been disbanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you interviewed and were you subject to questions about your political beliefs, including about the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The views you expressed as to this accused, were they positive or negative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were negative from their point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened so far as the interview or job interview was concerned and the consequence of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get the job because I didn't share the political opinions of the authorities in power at the time in the Republic of Serbia. But I believed then too that the state security was an institution protecting all the citizens of Serbia and not just the members of one party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first name of the man who interviewed you was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Others who were similarly contacted for possible recruitment by Frenki's secretary included?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Milorad Lukovic, Legija, and Nenad Bujosevic, the Big Rambo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness what is the basis of her conclusion that the reason for her not getting the job was her political views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when you filled in this form, you would have to wait for the contents to be checked out. After that, you would be called again to the building in Kneza Milosa street, and there I was told that I was not suitable because I had participated in the demonstrations of 1991, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Page 10, paragraph 52, money and support for the SDG. Did the SDG initially or at some stages have sponsors who provided money and supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who would provide money on a voluntary basis, and also goods. When I say "goods," I mean food, clothing, hygienic supplies and other supplies for the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The largest contributors, to your knowledge, being?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest sponsors of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were Giovani Di Stefano, also the Karic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Arkan also had some companies of his own. Did money from those companies go to the SDG company through which sponsors' money was channelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you if you could formulate that question a little more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there an SDG company, and if so, did donations pass through that company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some donations, if they were in the form of funds, would go through the SDG company. Not always all the funds. Some were given personally into the hands of Arkan. And in the event of objects or goods, they would directly arrive at our headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Arkan have companies himself; and if so, did those companies contribute money through the SDG company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDG company or, rather, in addition to that company, there were the Delije, the Delijes. It was a security agency and a trading company. And the funds from the cake shop and the bakery would be driven every morning to the Delije company which was situated in Vase Pelagica street, number 54 at Dedinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's turn to cash. Was cash received for the Tigers; and if so, where did it come from and who brought it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the sponsors or to the state security?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, no. State security now. Paragraph 54.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the Banja Luka operation, cash arrived at the headquarters from the state security in Belgrade. There were two ways in which this was done: Either one of the officers of the Serbian Volunteer Guard would go to fetch the money to the Kneza Milosa street, or Milanko would bring the cash to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you see cash brought? What sort of sums of money were involved on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the Banja Luka operation, money was delivered about ten times, and there was between 3 and 4 million Deutschmarks, because I and a couple of others counted the money. And we would place it in envelopes and pack these envelopes for the soldiers in Erdut, whereas the rest of the money would be placed by Arkan in the safe deposit -- safety deposit box in his office. So this was newly printed money that had just come out of the mint.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever see Arkan himself arriving with cash?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes he himself would go to fetch the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did he say to you, if anything, about the origin of that money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would just tell me that he had brought the money from the DB and that it was up to me to organise the counting of the money and to make sure that all soldiers in Erdut would receive their salaries out of those funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Next topic, Exhibit 432, tab 9, on the screen now, an entry from your diary. In December 1995, at a celebration for -- of St. Nikola, was there a distribution of pistols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander distributed to the officers and men who had in any way assisted the guards, he gave them pistols with an inscription. On the 19th of December 1995, which is St. Nikolas Day, and that is the patron saint of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think you took some part in organising the delivery of the pistols, but after the ceremony was over, did some of the Tigers with their pistols leave via Sid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them went via Novi Sad. Only three members went via Sid. There they were stopped by a patrol. The three of them, Sicko, Crvko and Kajman, plus the driver, they were taken into custody to the police station. I was called up, I called up the commander, and I'm referring to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, who said that I should tell the commander of the police station that they were Tigers. After that, the police commander released them but they kept the pistols. And then the next day I was told to call up Rodja, or Puzovic, from the republic SUP and to ask him to intervene for the pistols to be returned, and that is what happened. A couple of days later, the pistols were returned to the headquarters and they were returned to the owners who had received them on the 19th of December during the Slava or observation of St. Nikolas Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Exhibit on the screen, Exhibit 432, tab 10. This shows us what, please, Witness B-129?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something else. Are you referring to this that says the republic SUP? Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is noted here that I need to find Rodja in the republic SUP through the federal. Why is the federal mentioned? Because in a certain period of time, the republic SUP moved into the building of the federal SUP. So it was up to me to find this Rodja in room number 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then if we go to tab 11, please. What does this show us, if anything significant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows that Rodja or Puzovic, because I couldn't find them just then, that if I find them, I should connect him to office number 99, which was the code for the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll move on now then from these matters to some operational matters. Paragraphs 61 and 62. You've already told us about Bijeljina, Zvornik, Brcko, and Major Mauzer. But can we look at one particular photograph that's been exhibited before. It's Exhibit 411, tab 6. What can you tell us about this, please? This is a photograph from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry. Very well. Brcko then. What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the photograph is Srdjan Golubovic. His nickname was Max. He's a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and he was later involved in the Velika Kladusa operation. After this photograph, the commander was angry with Max that the photograph -- photographer had taken a photo of him trying to turn around a woman who was already dead when he approached her with his rifle to turn her over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was Max's response to that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he give any explanation for the death of the woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just said that when he arrived, she had already been -- she had already passed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraph 65. Did you see anything of Radovan Stojicic, known as Badza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you learn of his relationship or the development of his relationship with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that during the operation in Eastern Slavonia during 1991, they were very close. And there is even a photograph of the two of them together in the camp at Erdut. However, during 1993, that is the end of 1993 and the beginning the 1994, Badza, and I'm referring to Stojicic, took over the camp of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in Erdut, and Arkan was furious about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the -- apart from the fact the camp was taken over, what was his particular concern at what had happened and what was his view on the camp that was being taken over? What was his view of its professionalism or modernity or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Arkan was unhappy that Badza had taken over the camp. What was Arkan's view of his contribution to the camp and of what sort of camp he had created?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first camp of the Serbian Volunteer Guard was one of the most modern camps in the former Yugoslavia, because it was devised by Arkan as a training facility for the special unit. And there was what was called as a rubber town inside it. People who are well-versed in military matters will know what I'm talking about when I refer to a rubber town as related to a training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Very well. Did Arkan's other interests, including his interests in smuggling, have anything to do with the change in relationship between him and Badza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on several occasions in front of us at the headquarters, he said that smuggling most influenced their relationship because, as he said - and I'm meaning Arkan - Badza wants to keep everything to himself and for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In May of 1995, was Arkan informed that help was needed in the Krajina region as a result of Operation Flash, and was it this that led to the reopening of the camp or of a camp at Erdut in any event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this second facility was in slightly a different position, I think. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this second camp was along the riverbank itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once this had been opened, did you have to visit it regularly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go there often. And if Arkan was at the front, it was my job to go there every weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you take supplies from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take the supplies too when I went, although there was a kombi van which would go every day from Erdut to Belgrade and vice versa, Belgrade-Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Very well, let's go back a bit in time now and look at Velika Kladusa more comprehensively. On the 4th of November, 1994, did Arkan inform you of something, or did Arkan inform the Tigers generally of something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He informed me that I was to call up people from a list. And I did call them up and told them to come to headquarters. They all came, they all responded, and nobody asked why. After that, the commander told me that Frenki had told him that he needed men to resupply his unit. In the space of two days, we rallied up about 40 men. At the time, I myself did not know where they were going. On the 4th of November, 1994, that first group of men left. Their leader, that is to say the commander of that unit, was Legija, and in the unit was Suca and Big Rambo and others. According to their stories, they first went to a camp of the MUP of Serbia or DB of Serbia, which was located on Mount Tara, Bajina Basta. And after spending seven days there, they were transferred to Velika Kladusa itself. In that period of time, I myself learnt where they were, but otherwise it was a secret operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court can see the location of Velika Kladusa on tab 20 on the far western side -- left-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Reflecting the secrecy, how were the men who went dressed? What happened to -- how were they dressed first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all on their way there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they were dressed in their civilian clothing. When they arrived, when the bus arrived, the MUP of Serbia bus to pick them up from in front of our headquarters, and Arkan himself told them, actually, that they could use and would use uniforms, the uniforms of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, but that they were not allowed to place any insignia with the Tigers on their arms. No arm patches with the tiger insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was Arkan able to go himself? If not, who led the operation in Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan was not able to go there himself because most of the people knew what Arkan looked like. So the Tigers were led by Legija, and the members of the DB were led by Radojica Bozovic, nicknamed Raja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was the first deployment. Was there a second group of Tigers that went off? Paragraph 77. And I'll come back to look at the exhibits in a second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The second group left on the 18th of November, 1994. It was a smaller group. There were a little under 20 men in it. And their leader, their commander, was Colonel Mihajlo Ulemek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us about the departure from Mount Tara, but I'm not sure if you've told us -- you have. You told us it was a Serb DB bus.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's look at a couple of exhibits before me move on. Exhibit 432, tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you could help me. Could you remind me of the relationship between Milorad Ulemek and Mihajlo Ulemek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I'll ask the witness to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mihajlo Ulemek and Milorad Ulemek are two different people. Mihajlo Ulemek was a man of about 60 years of age, and from the very beginning, that is to say from 1991, he was in the Serb Volunteer Guard, whereas Milorad Ulemek is the Milorad Lukovic or Legija man, and he joined the SDB later. Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged to Ms. Pack for reminding me that we can find this in your chart, I hope. Tab 4. You can see them both there, on the second to last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we now look at tab 12. If the witness can have the -- or we can see the Cyrillic version on the screen. And if the English version can be available perhaps on the overhead projector, and we can switch to that for those who will be following in English. This document, dated the 26th of February, 1995, later than the period you've been dealing with so far, is this a document that you had not seen before you came here to prepare to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not seen it. I see it now for the first time. However, Legija, and I mean Milorad Lukovic, with the Serb Volunteer Guard, was in Velika Kladusa. With part of it, anyway. And he was there right up until August 1995, which means up to the Storm operation. They were there all the time. Some people would go on leave for a time and return, but Legija and most of the unit was there permanently in Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this document from him, headed "Regulating Subordination in the Army of Western Bosnia," can you help us with its or its interpretation? It deals with forming and organising the ZB army, "A system of command and control was established to which the Pauk Command was our superior command." Are you in a position to explain that in a little more detail for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The Pauk operation in the SDG meant a clandestine operation waged in Velika Kladusa. And that was also, when I called up to begin with, the DB, when I would say the word "Pauk," they would transfer me to Sladjana's or, rather, Frenki's office. So Pauk was the code name of the operation which included the state security and the SDG. In the lower bottom corner, we have Colonel Legija's signature. At the time, he was a colonel, but after the Velika Kladusa operation, which means in August, when he returned, he was accorded the rank of general, general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And although you probably made this clear, the purpose of this operation was what so far as Fikret Abdic's men were concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation consisted of the following: The DB and the SDG trained his men, although in the final instance it didn't boil down to that. Actually, they had two killed fighters. So they also took part in the operations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We move on to tab 13, with His Honour Judge Kwon's question just in mind. We now see a document a little earlier in time, the 18th of December, 1994, the content of which may not be particularly significant or weighty, but it's signed by Mihajlo Ulemek. It comes from combat group 2, and it authorises somebody called Sead Cufurovic to drive his Zastava 648 vehicle with provisions, on a stretch of road between Ponikve and Topusko. The significance for you of this document which you hadn't seen before coming here, in light of what you've been able to tell us about an operation known as Pauk.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this document. I've never seen it, I am looking at it now for the first time. Topusko was a place where the Guard and all its members would go out for supplies - for example, if they needed any kind of supplies or food - and this was signed by Mihajlo Ulemek, as we see, because he was the only man who could give permission as the boss, as the head of the military police, for anybody to move around in that part of the territory. And another thing that links this document with the SDG is the last sentence, in which he says that he will be escorted by Cica, Cica Pera. Not Petar Cica but Cica Pera. And Cica Pera was a member of the SDG who, with another group, went to Velika Kladusa. So he went with Mihajlo Ulemek in this second group. They went to Velika Kladusa together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 80. Were the Tigers involved with another group in Kladusa led by Raja Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They acted together over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's a Serbian DB group. Did they wear red berets, or were they known as Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were known as the Red Berets. Now, whether they actually wore red berets in Velika Kladusa, I can't really say, I can't answer that question. Although I do know that the Tigers, during the Velika Kladusa operation, wore caps which looked like the ranger type of cap. So they weren't the standard type, usual type of cap worn by the army, by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to those, that group by Bozovic, was there a group from Banja Luka; and if so, by whom was that led?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a group led by Ljuban Ecim. It was a group from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the field, who had superiority as between Legija and Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how do you attribute him to the DB? How do you know he was of the DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the operation, the Velika Kladusa operation, when Radojica Bozovic would come to Belgrade, he would come to us at headquarters too. And he said he had come to greet us and to convey to the commanders that his fighters were okay and ask whether they needed anything or we needed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us of Arkan's difficulties in going to Velika Kladusa. What about Frenki? Did he go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Frenki did go to Velika Kladusa. I know that from what the members of the SDG said. And I also know it because Sladjana told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When Tigers returned from Velika Kladusa in the course of this operation, can you tell us what they had to do about their personal documentation, how they were contacted when they had to return, and also what was done and through what organisation if they were ever to receive parcels, things like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific and concrete when asking your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll break them down into smaller questions. When they came back from the front, what did they do with their personal identifications, their Tiger identifications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. When they went on leave, which would usually last about a fortnight, the SDG ID cards, I mean the SDG ID cards, they would drop those off at the headquarters, and in return, they would receive their own personal documents, IDs. And a day or two before leaving again, Sladjana would call me up and tell me to get them ready in the next two days. Usually a bus would arrive at about 7.00 in the morning, and then the procedure would be the same; they would leave their IDs and take up the SDG ID cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, the last part of the three-part question I asked you earlier: If somebody wanted to send something to a Tiger when he was in Velika Kladusa, how was that organised? A parcel, for example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call up Sladjana and ask her if possible to either send a message or a letter or a parcel. She never refused. That means that the driver would take it to the building in Kneza Milosa street, and she says the driver would usually come out, she would take over the package or whatever, and she would give it to the driver to take to the person, to transport to the person in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How were those Tigers fighting for Fikret -- fighting to -- or assisting Fikret Abdic? How were they paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their monthly salary amounted to 1.500 German marks which at that time was a great deal of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did the money come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it came from; how do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did Fikret Abdic get the money to pay them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you hear from people at the front about the mechanism whereby the money was handed over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they would be in the field, Legija would go into the building where Fikret Abdic was, he would take the money, and afterwards he would pay out the money to all the soldiers. If there were wounded soldiers, then the money would go via the DB and reach our headquarters, and later on I would hand the money out to the wounded soldiers, that money that had come from Velika Kladusa. Sometimes I would send a driver or one of the other wounded soldiers, because all the soldiers knew where our offices were, and then one of the wounded soldiers would go and take the money and distribute it amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What Tiger or DB casualties were there in Velika Kladusa? Paragraphs 87 and 88.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tigers had two casualties; Dimitrije Jasek, Mitar, and Jugoslav Micic, Juka. Whereas on the DB side there was a high-ranking officer who was killed, Kojic, and they later named the Kula camp after him. I'm thinking of the JSO camp in Kula.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After our own fighters were killed, and I'm thinking about Dimitrije Jasek and Jugoslav Micic, we weren't allowed to place an obituary saying where they had died, where they had been killed. All we could say was they had died defending Serb lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were prisoners detained in the Kladusa area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who operated the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the tales told by the wounded soldiers, everybody was in charge of the prison; Fikret's men, the DB men, and members of the Guard, because they were all active there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, according to what you were told, was the treatment of the prisoners like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the prisoners succumbed to their wounds received from beatings several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've dealt with the ranger hats worn by the Tigers in Velika Kladusa, so I'll turn to another topic. Mihalj Kertes, what involvement if any did he have with Arkan that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Mihalj Kertes was always called when there was a truck coming in from Bulgaria or Macedonia and when it had problems at the border crossing. The truck was either carrying cigarettes or alcoholic beverages. After that, a gentleman, Dejan Lekic from Transped, a state company, transport company, would call me up and tell me to tell Zeljko to call Kertes. Dejan Lekic would always give me the number of the number plates of the truck and the name of the driver driving it. Then I would convey this to the commander, and in the course of the day the truck would be allowed to pass the border crossing. After that, from the border crossing onwards, the truck would be driven straight to Erdut, and it would be like -- actually, it didn't undergo any customs procedure. They would just place a stamp signifying that the goods had entered Eastern Slavonia, and part of the goods would be kept at the duty free shop at the petrol pump in Erdut, whereas most of the goods would be returned to Serbia and sold there, sold to people who would come to our headquarters and who knew that we had the goods, that the goods were available. So those cigarettes and the whisky would come from Erdut in a kombi van, in one of our own kombi vans that would communicate between Erdut and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this trafficking in tobacco and alcohol was in reality Arkan's business, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he, to your knowledge, use the money from that business to support in part the guards by uniforms or supplies or things like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because all the money was kept at the headquarters. It would be kept in a safe. And whenever the SDG did not -- company did not have any money to pay for something that it needed to pay, they would take the money out of the safe deposit and pay for the medicines, uniforms, clothing, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: An associated topic, tab 14. Yes, tab 14. Was there a general known to you called Loncar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Dusko Loncar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Just to help us, is this the Loncar who turns up in Kosovo? Is there a different one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one moment. First of all, it's a question I want to ask the witness about that and I'll come to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What do you know about this general's origins and the force for which he was in service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dusan Loncar was commander of the Sremska Baranska Corps in Eastern Slavonia during 1995. He is a man who was at the time about 60 years of age. So I'm talking about the period of 1995. He was in charge of the Yugoslav army in Eastern Slavonia. And the guards were often told to contact him because he supplied us with weapons, oil. When I say "oil," I mean fuel for vehicles. And a part of the money was also received from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the position about this particular officer is that he is the person who features later, and we do have material to connect him with the 40th personnel centre in Belgrade. That will be before you in due course if it's not before you already. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we look at tab 14 of Exhibit 432, tell us about that, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please, insofar as it requires much explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called up from Erdut by a colonel called Puki. I can't remember his proper name and surname. He was in charge of the administration in our centre, and he asked me to convey to the commander that General Loncar was stalling with the salaries. What he meant was that General Loncar was not providing the amount of money that the Yugoslav army provided for the soldiers in the Serbian Volunteer Guards who were in Erdut. He was not providing the money in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've dealt with money and in your earlier answer dealing with General Loncar, you dealt with weapons and oil in general terms. Did the weaponry include heavy weaponry and ammunition that he supplied or organised the supply of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean when you say "heavy weaponry"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he supply all the weaponry that came to Erdut in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rifles, automatic, semi-automatic, grenades, explosives. There were no tanks or anything like that, because they were not needed for operations by the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this was all, as you understood it, coming from the VJ at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Loncar's headquarters was where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loncar's headquarters, where he acted together with Legija, was in Trpinja. It's a small locality in Eastern Slavonia. And the two of them shared the command headquarters as far as Eastern Slavonia was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And of course Puki has appeared in the evidence. I seem to remember his death was one of the matters which was dealt with. I may be wrong about that, but a man called himself Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is ahead of me there on recollection, but I'll look it up for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be convenient to move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's now time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've made very good progress, I think. We've got four pages to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- which I'll try and take as swiftly as I can. There are no more exhibits that will take time, I think, of the kind -- of the intercept kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we must complete this witness tomorrow, so if you would go as rapidly as possible with the evidence in chief, that will leave us with two and a bit hours for cross-examination, if it's required to take that long. Any time over, we can deal with administrative matters. Witness B-129, I should have told you before, or should have warned you: Don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, please, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back tomorrow morning at 9.00 to finish your evidence. We will adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of April, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
